title: The LORD Returns to Jerusalem
sum: Two months after Haggai's first message, and while the Temple builders are at work, Zechariah receives his first word: the LORD was angry with your ancestors, so do not be like them. Turn back to me, and I will turn back to you. The ancestors are dead, and so are the earlier prophets, but the prophets' words caught up with them, and they admitted it (1:1-6).

On the night of 15 February 519 BC, Zechariah sees a man on a red horse among myrtle trees, with riders who have walked the earth and found it quiet (1:7-17). The angel of the LORD asks how long the LORD will withhold compassion from Jerusalem, and the LORD answers with comforting words: he is jealous for Zion, he has come back to Jerusalem, his house will be rebuilt and a measuring line stretched over the city. In a second vision four horns, which scattered Judah, meet four craftsmen who have come to throw them down (1:18-21).
readings: Read as a message to builders

The book opens with a call that makes sense for a community that has started the Temple and is not sure its labor means anything. The LORD's return is the reason to continue, and the quiet world is the reason to wait.
Read as the opening of a pattern

The ring of horses in 1:8 and chariots in 6:1-8 frames eight visions in which the LORD returns, the city is measured, the priest is cleansed, the light is supplied, the land is purged and the nations are judged.

views.H: The first dated word (late October to late November 520) comes while the Temple walls rise, and the visions (15 February 519) come five months after work began. The "seventy years" are about 67 since 586. Darius I had put down the revolts of 522-521; in 519 the empire was calm, which was a problem for those who expected a shaking (Haggai 2:6-7, 21-22). The Temple was finished in March 515 (Ezra 6:15).
views.C: Most critical commentators take 1:1-6 as an introduction written after the visions to give them a call to repentance as a frame, and the visions as Zechariah's core. The four horns and craftsmen (1:18-21) are Hebrew 2:1-4. The Greek has "mountains" for "myrtle trees" (1:8, 10, 11) and "his holy clouds" later (2:13). The visions follow a set form, and later chapters add oracles to them.
views.J: The Talmud counts Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi as the last prophets (Yoma 9b) and makes the four craftsmen four figures of the end: the Messiah son of David, the Messiah son of Joseph, Elijah and the righteous priest (Sukkah 52b). Jewish commentators usually read the four horns as the empires that ruled Israel. The seventy years are Jeremiah's.
views.X: Calvin, on 1:7-11, says that if the angel is taken to be Christ, the idea fits the usual language of Scripture, since Christ is the head of the angels. The "comforting words" (1:13) have often been heard as the gospel's first note, and the measuring line (1:16) as the building of the church. These are receptions.
views.F: The promise that "once more the LORD will comfort Zion, and once more he will choose Jerusalem" (1:17) was read by some as not yet fulfilled in 519 or since. Premillennial and dispensationalist readers connect the measuring line with a restored Jerusalem and temple at the end (Ezekiel 40-48); others hold the promise fulfilled in Christ and the church.

deep.h: Who is the angel of the LORD?
deep.b: In 1:8-12 the rider, the man among the myrtles and the angel of the LORD seem to be one figure, and he speaks to the LORD and receives an answer from him. In Genesis 16:7-13, Exodus 3:2-6 and Judges 6:11-24 the angel of the LORD speaks as the LORD himself and is hard to tell from him, but in Zechariah the angel and the LORD are two: the angel asks, the LORD answers. Jewish readers take the figure as the greatest of the angels. Christian writers have often taken him as the Son of God before his birth, and Calvin, on 3:1-2, takes the angel before whom Joshua stood to be Christ. Modern scholars point out that in Zechariah the angel is a member of the heavenly council, a go-between, and that the book keeps the LORD at a distance from the earth.

echoes: Haggai 1:14; Haggai 2:6-9; Jeremiah 25:11-12; Jeremiah 29:10; Isaiah 40:1; Ezekiel 40:3; Job 1:6-7; Revelation 6:1-8; 2 Chronicles 36:20-21; Deuteronomy 28

settings.by: The LORD, through Zechariah son of Berechiah, the prophet
settings.to: The people of the province of Judah (Yehud), the community around Jerusalem, whose "ancestors" had been warned by the earlier prophets and then judged
settings.when: Late October to late November 520 BC (the eighth month of Darius's second year), about two months after Haggai's first message and a month after work on the Temple started
settings.why: To make the people of the returned community see that the exile was not an accident: the earlier prophets had warned, and what they said came true. It opens the book with an invitation and a promise: return to the LORD, and he will return to you. Knowing the hearers (a poor community building a Temple that looks small) turns the call from a scolding into the first step toward the comfort that follows.
views: Zechariah gave this word at the start of his work, to the same people Haggai had stirred.
Many critical scholars hold that the opening was composed or shaped later as a frame for the visions, in the same dated style as Haggai.

settings.what: The vision of the riders among the myrtle trees
settings.by: Zechariah, who sees the vision; the angel of the LORD and the LORD himself speak
settings.to: Zechariah first, then the people of Judah and Jerusalem, who hear the report and the messages "Call out" (1:14, 17)
settings.when: The night of 15 February 519 BC (24 Shebat, the eleventh month), five months after work began
settings.why: To answer the question the Temple builders were asking: how long? The world was quiet, the Temple was half built, and the great shaking Haggai had promised had not come. The vision shows that heaven has already heard the question and that the LORD's answer is comfort and jealousy for Zion.
views: The book tells those at work on the Temple that the work is part of a larger turning of the LORD to Jerusalem.

settings.what: The four horns and the four craftsmen
settings.to: The community of Judah, a people who had been scattered and hemmed in by stronger nations
settings.why: To assure a small, powerless province that the powers that scattered it will themselves be dismantled. The nations are not named, so any later hearer can find their own enemy in the horns.
views: The horns are Assyria, Egypt, Babylon and another, or four great empires in turn.
Four is the number of the four directions; the horns are all the hostile nations.

title: A City Without Walls
sum: A man with a measuring cord is on his way to measure Jerusalem, but an angel sends word to him: the city will be too full of people and animals for walls, and the LORD himself will be a wall of fire around it and its glory inside (2:1-5). In the English numbering, this chapter has 13 verses; in Hebrew it is 2:5-17.

A poem follows: a call to the exiles to leave the north and Babylon, the promise that the nations that plundered Zion will be plundered, a summons to joy ("I am about to come, and I will make my home among you"), a promise that many nations will join themselves to the LORD, and a command to the whole world to be silent because the LORD has stirred himself (2:6-13).

views.H: In 519 BC Jerusalem was a small town of a few thousand people on the old City of David ridge, and its walls were down (Nehemiah 1:3). Many Jews remained in Babylon, and 2:6-7 calls them to come. The promise of nations joining the LORD (2:11) had no sign of coming true. Nehemiah rebuilt the walls in 445.
views.C: Scholars think 2:6-13 may be a separate oracle attached to the vision, and that 2:10-13 is a hymn of the LORD's coming. The speaker who says "the LORD has sent me" in 2:8-11 is unexplained. The Greek has "fruitfully inhabited" in 2:4 and "his holy clouds" in 2:13. The Hebrew chapter 2 begins at English 1:18 (English 2:1 is Hebrew 2:5), and English 2:10 begins the haftarah of Hanukkah (Hebrew 2:14).
views.J: Jewish tradition reads 2:10-13 (Hebrew 2:14-17) as the haftarah of the Sabbath of Hanukkah, with the promise "not by strength" (4:6) to follow. The Shekhinah, the divine presence, takes its name from the verb "make my home" (2:10). The pupil of the eye is Israel, which the nations touch at their peril.
views.X: Christians read "I will make my home among you" in light of John 1:14, and "many nations will join themselves to the LORD" of the church (Ephesians 2). Revelation 18:4 uses "Come out of her, my people" of a later Babylon. The Vulgate's "my eye" (2:8) made the verse a promise that God treats his people's hurt as his own.
views.F: The promise that the LORD will come to live in the midst of Jerusalem and that many nations will join him (2:10-11) is read as still to come by Dispensationalist and many premillennial readers (the millennial kingdom), by Jewish readers (the days of the Messiah) and by some others as the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21).

echoes: Ezekiel 40:3; Ezekiel 43:1-5; Isaiah 4:5; Isaiah 48:20; Isaiah 52:11; Jeremiah 51:6; Isaiah 49:19-20; Revelation 18:4; Revelation 21:2-3; John 1:14; Zephaniah 3:14-17; Deuteronomy 32:10

settings.what: The vision of the man with the measuring cord
settings.to: The people of Jerusalem and Judah, living in a small city with broken walls, who would hear it from the prophet
settings.why: To tell people who counted every stone and feared the empire that the real defense of the city was not a wall but the LORD himself, and that the city would outgrow any wall. It answers the worry that the city is too small and unprotected.
views: The city will fill with people and animals beyond its old limits.
Some Jewish and Christian readers hear a warning against trusting in walls instead of God. Nehemiah's later wall-building (Nehemiah 2-6) shows the promise was not read as forbidding walls.

settings.what: The call to leave Babylon and the promise of the LORD's coming
settings.by: The LORD, through Zechariah and the speaker who says "the LORD has sent me"
settings.to: The Jews still living in Babylon and the north (2:6-7), then "Daughter Zion" and the nations (2:10-13)
settings.when: The same night, 15 February 519 BC, as the continuation of the vision
settings.why: To call the exiles home and to tell those at home that the LORD himself is returning. Hearers who had sent word to the exiles or waited for them would hear it as a summons: come, build, and see the nations drawn to the LORD.
views: The "you" of 2:6-7 is the Jewish community in Babylon.
In 2:13, "all flesh" is called to silence, so the poem ends with a call to all humanity.

title: Joshua, the Accuser and the Clean Turban
sum: In a heavenly courtroom, Joshua the high priest stands before the angel of the LORD in filthy clothes, and the Accuser stands at his right side to charge him. The LORD silences the Accuser ("May the LORD rebuke you") and calls Joshua a piece of firewood snatched from the fire. The angel orders the filthy clothes removed, announces "I have taken your guilt away from you," and has Joshua dressed in fine robes and a clean turban (3:1-5).

Then comes a charge: if Joshua walks in the LORD's ways and carries out his duty, he will govern the house and be given a place among "these who stand here" (heavenly attendants, or priests; the Hebrew allows either). Joshua and the priests are a sign of the Branch, the LORD's servant, whom the LORD is about to bring. A stone with seven eyes is set before Joshua, and the LORD will carve it and remove the land's guilt in one day. On that day neighbors will call to neighbors to come and sit under a vine and a fig tree (3:6-10).
readings: Read as a vision of the priesthood
The scene concerns the Temple's priests and the worship that will begin when the building is complete. The cleansing makes the high priest fit to serve.
Read as a vision of the nation
Joshua stands for the people: a survivor of the fire, charged, accused and forgiven because the LORD has chosen Jerusalem.
Read as a promise of a future cleansing
The Branch and the single day (3:8-9) point beyond Joshua to a day when the land's guilt is removed, read by Jews as Yom Kippur or the end of days and by Christians as the cross.

views.H: Joshua son of Jehozadak was the first high priest of the second Temple (Ezra 3:2; Haggai 1:1). The scene, dated to the night of 15 February 519, comes while the Temple is being built and before the Temple building is finished (the altar had been in use since 538: Ezra 3:2-6). The Accuser stands for the charges that could be brought: that the priests were unfit after exile, and that Judah did not deserve a rebuilt Temple.
views.C: Critics ask how a heavenly Accuser, found only in Job, here and in 1 Chronicles 21:1, relates to the later Satan. Some see 3:1-10 as made of several parts: the court scene (3:1-5), a charge to Joshua (3:6-7) and an appendix about the Branch and the stone (3:8-10), with the Greek's "Anatolē" for Branch. The Dead Sea scroll 4Q80 preserves most of 3:2-10, with only spelling differences in the printout.
views.J: Jewish tradition read the scene with the priesthood in mind: Sanhedrin 93a explains the filthy clothes by Joshua's sons' marriages to women unfit for priests. The Targum calls the Branch "my servant the Messiah." The Satan is a prosecuting angel in God's service, as in Job. The Day of Atonement frames the single day (3:9).
views.X: Justin Martyr (Dialogue 115-116) read Joshua, whose name is Jesus in Greek, as a picture of Jesus Christ and his people. The Reformers read the new clothing as free pardon, and the Fathers saw the Accuser as the devil. Jude 9 echoes 3:2, and Revelation 12:10 calls the devil the accuser. The Branch is Christ (Luke 1:78). These are receptions.
views.F: Some read 3:8-10 as still to come: the coming of the Branch (the Messiah), a single day of cleansing (at the second coming, in dispensationalist and premillennial readings, or on the Day of Atonement of the end) and a peace in which each person invites his neighbor under the vine and the fig tree.

deep.h: The Accuser in the Hebrew Bible
deep.b: The word satan means an adversary, a person or thing that stands in someone's way: the angel who blocks Balaam (Numbers 22:22), Hadad and Rezon against Solomon (1 Kings 11:14, 23), David as a possible adversary of the Philistines (1 Samuel 29:4). With the article, hassatan, it names a role in the court of God: the one who tests and accuses. In Job 1-2 he is among "the sons of God" and acts only with God's leave. In Zechariah 3 he is the prosecutor in a trial. In 1 Chronicles 21:1 "Satan" (no article) stirs up David to count the people, where the older parallel in 2 Samuel 24:1 says the LORD's anger did. The New Testament's devil, an enemy of God ruling the world, is much more developed (Matthew 4; John 12:31; Revelation 12). How the earlier figure became the later is debated: gradual development within Israel, influence from Persian dualism, or Greek-era apocalyptic thought.
deep.refs: Numbers 22:22; 1 Samuel 29:4; 1 Kings 11:14; 1 Chronicles 21:1; 2 Samuel 24:1; Job 1:6-12; Job 2:1-7; Zechariah 3:1-2; Revelation 12:9-10

deep.b: Zechariah uses the Branch (tsemach) twice, at 3:8 and 6:12, both times as a name ("my servant, the Branch"; "a man whose name is Branch"). Jeremiah had used it twice for a righteous Davidic king (Jeremiah 23:5; Jeremiah 33:15), and Isaiah has "the LORD's branch" at 4:2 and a shoot from Jesse's stump at 11:1 (different words). The Greek translates the word with anatolē, "rising" or "dawn," which is why Luke 1:78 can speak of "the Dawn from on high." For Zechariah the name fits Zerubbabel, who is the Davidic governor and temple builder; the book does not make him a king. After Zerubbabel the name became a title of the expected Messiah in Jewish and Christian reading. The topic on the Branch follows it through Jeremiah, Isaiah and Zechariah.
deep.refs: Jeremiah 23:5; Jeremiah 33:15; Isaiah 4:2; Isaiah 11:1; Zechariah 3:8; Zechariah 6:12; Luke 1:78

echoes: Job 1:6-12; 1 Chronicles 21:1; Psalm 109:6; Amos 4:11; Leviticus 16; Isaiah 6:6-7; Isaiah 61:10; Jude 9; Revelation 12:10; Revelation 7:14; Romans 8:33-34; Hebrews 7:27; Micah 4:4; 1 Kings 4:25

settings.what: The vision of Joshua, the Accuser and the clean turban, with the charge to Joshua and the promise of the Branch
settings.by: Zechariah (the vision); the LORD, the angel of the LORD and the Accuser in the scene
settings.to: Joshua the high priest and the priests who sit before him ("your companions," 3:8), and through them the people of Judah
settings.when: The night of 15 February 519 BC, while the Temple was under construction and before it could be used
settings.why: To tell the priests and people that their right to serve is the LORD's gift, not their record. A Temple built by a priesthood that was ashamed of its past, in a city that was a survivor of fire, needed to hear that the charge against them had been silenced and the guilt taken away. The charge to walk in the LORD's ways answers that gift with a duty, and the promise of the Branch points to a day beyond the building.
views: The first hearers are the high priest and his fellow priests; they are the ones addressed as "you" in 3:6-10.
Joshua stands for the people, the plucked-out log is Judah, and the one day removes the guilt of "this land" (3:9).
Some critics see 3:8-10 as added after Zerubbabel's time, shifting the focus from a governor to a coming king.

traditions.q: What does the change of clothes in Zechariah 3:4 teach about how God makes a sinner right with him?
views: The guilt is taken away before Joshua does anything: God declares the sinner free for Christ's sake alone, as Article 4 of the Augsburg Confession says we are justified freely for Christ's sake through faith. The Lutheran use of the scene is of a pardon that comes from outside the person. Luther gave Latin lectures on Zechariah in 1525-26, and his German work on the prophet appeared in December 1527.

Forgiveness comes first and the clothing second. Calvin, on 3:4, notes that the angel first says the iniquity has been taken away and then promises the change of clothing, and he ties the change to God's gratuitous remission. The Westminster Confession (11.1) speaks of God "imputing the obedience and satisfaction of Christ" to the sinner.

The Catechism (1989) teaches that justification is not only the remission of sins but also the sanctification and renewal of the interior man. The taking away of guilt and the new clothing are one gift that forgives and renews.

title: Not by Strength and Not by Force
sum: The angel wakes Zechariah like a man woken from sleep and shows him a gold lampstand with a bowl on top, seven lamps with pipes, and two olive trees standing beside it. The prophet does not know what the vision means (4:1-5). The answer is a word to Zerubbabel: "Not by strength and not by force, but by my Spirit." The great mountain will become level ground, Zerubbabel will bring out the top stone to shouts of "Favor, favor to it!", his own hands founded the house and his hands will bring it to completion (4:6-10a).

The seven lamps are the seven eyes of the LORD, roving over all the earth. The prophet asks twice what the two olive trees are and learns that they are "the two sons of fresh oil who stand by the Lord of the whole earth" (4:10b-14).
readings: Read as encouragement for builders
The oil flows by itself, and the LORD's Spirit provides what the builders lack. The vision is to a small community whose Temple looks like nothing (Haggai 2:3).
Read as a vision of two leaders
The two olive trees are the governor and the high priest, the two on whom the community depends, shown as the channels of the LORD's supply.
Read as a vision of the end

The lampstand and the two trees recur in Revelation 1:12, 20 and 11:4, where the lampstands are the churches and the two witnesses. Christian readers hear the lamp of the church and the two witnesses of the last days.

views.H: The ground is the building of the Temple under Zerubbabel, after the foundation ceremony of 18 December 520, and before its completion in Darius's sixth year (Ezra 6:15). Zerubbabel was a grandson of King Jehoiachin and governor of Yehud under Darius, and the earliest hopes of a Davidic restoration clung to him. The Persian court in 519 was calm after the revolts of 522-521.
views.C: Scholars often treat 4:6-10a as a separate oracle inserted into the lampstand vision, because it interrupts the explanation of the trees (4:4-5 continues in 4:11-14) and speaks of Zerubbabel, not the lampstand. The Hebrew has "I said" (Qere) or "he said" (Ketiv) at 4:2. The Greek reads "the stone of the inheritance" for "the top stone" (4:7).
views.J: Jewish tradition reads 4:6 as the theme of the haftarah for the Sabbath of Hanukkah (Hebrew 2:14 to 4:7), where the lampstand matches the menorah of the festival. The two olive trees are read as the two leaders, Zerubbabel and Joshua, and in later tradition also as two Messiahs.
views.X: Christians read the lampstand as the church (Revelation 1:20), the oil as the Holy Spirit, and the verse "Not by strength, but by my Spirit" as a rule for the church's mission. The two olive trees became the two witnesses (Revelation 11:4). Zerubbabel the temple builder has been read as a type of Christ the builder of the church.
views.F: Some read the two olive trees as the two witnesses of the last days (Revelation 11), and the "top stone" as the Messiah placed at the end. Most commentators hold that Zechariah 4 itself speaks only of the second Temple, and that the future reading belongs to Revelation's use of it.

deep.h: "Not by might": a slogan and its setting
deep.b: Zechariah 4:6 is among the best-known verses of the minor prophets, often printed on posters and used as a motto for relying on God. The Hebrew says lo vechayil velo vekoach ki im beruchi: "not by army (or strength) and not by force, but by my Spirit." It is spoken to a governor from David's line, in a Persian province, about a building project. A few years earlier there had been revolts in the empire, and some Jews could have hoped for a rebellion led by a Davidic prince (Haggai 2:21-23). The prophet tells Zerubbabel that the Temple will rise by the LORD's power and not by arms. That does not mean human work is useless: "his hands will bring it to completion" (4:9). It also says nothing about armies in general; the same book looks forward to the LORD's war against nations (14:1-3). In Christian use the verse has often been applied to evangelism and church planting, which is a reception and not what the Hebrew first said.
deep.refs: Haggai 2:21-23; Zechariah 4:9; Zechariah 12:1-9; Ezra 6:6-12; Isaiah 11:2; Ezekiel 36:27

echoes: Exodus 25:31-40; 1 Kings 7:49; Haggai 2:3-5; Haggai 2:23; Isaiah 11:2; 2 Chronicles 16:9; Revelation 1:12; Revelation 1:20; Revelation 4:5; Revelation 5:6; Revelation 11:4; Matthew 17:20; Ezra 3:12-13

settings.what: The vision of the lampstand and two olive trees
settings.by: Zechariah (the vision); the angel who spoke with him
settings.to: Zechariah, who passes it to Zerubbabel, Joshua and the Temple builders
settings.why: To show a community working on a Temple that its light would be fed from a source that does not run out.

settings.what: The word of the LORD to Zerubbabel
settings.by: The LORD of Armies, through the angel
settings.to: Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and the people who were building with him
settings.when: The night of 15 February 519 BC, about five months after the work began
settings.why: To strengthen the governor at a moment when the Temple looked small and the opposition was large (Ezra 4-5). Zerubbabel needed to be told that the means would be the LORD's Spirit, that the obstacle would become a plain, that his own hands would finish the work, and that nobody should look down on a modest start.
views: The oracle encourages a governor facing opposition.
The oracle also warns the Davidic governor away from a political uprising, trusting the LORD's Spirit instead.

settings.what: The meaning of the olive trees
settings.by: The angel who spoke with Zechariah
settings.when: The same night, after the word to Zerubbabel
settings.why: To name the two leaders as the channels through which the LORD's supply reached the community, and to tell the people that both leaders stand before the LORD of the whole earth, not before the Persian king.
views: Some read the trees as the two prophets.
Jewish and Qumran expectation of a royal and a priestly Messiah, applied later.

title: The Flying Scroll and the Basket
sum: Zechariah sees a huge scroll, 20 cubits by 10, flying over the land. The angel says it carries the curse against everyone who steals and everyone who swears falsely by the LORD's name. The LORD sends it into the house of each, where it stays and consumes the house, timbers and stones (5:1-4).

Then a round measuring basket, an ephah, goes out. A lead lid is lifted and a woman is sitting inside: "This is Wickedness." The angel pushes her down and shuts the lid with the lead weight. Two women with wings like a stork's carry the basket up between earth and sky, to build a house for it in the land of Shinar, where it will be set down on its own base (5:5-11).
readings: Read as the cleansing of the land

The scroll and the ephah are two ways of removing sin: the judgment of the guilty, and the exile of Wickedness itself. They answer 3:9, where the LORD promises to remove the guilt of the land in a single day.
Read as a vision about commerce and the Temple
Theft, false oath and the ephah are the wrongs of the market. The Temple's standard (20 by 10 cubits) goes out as a rule over the whole economy.
Read as a vision about idols and Babylon
Wickedness in the ephah is the cult figure of a foreign god sent home to Shinar, where she belongs and has her own temple.

views.H: The visions come in 519, when Judah had been through years of poor harvests and conflict between neighbors (Haggai 1:6, 9-11; Zechariah 8:10). Theft and false oaths belong to a society under strain; Nehemiah 5 later shows the lending abuses of the same community. Shinar is Babylonia; many Jews were still there.
views.C: Scholars ask what the woman is: the personification of sin, a goddess, or the land's corruption. They also ask whether 5:5-11 is a later addition, whether the scroll and the ephah belong together, and what the Greek's "sickle" shows. The Hebrew of 5:3 "cleaned out" is hard. The Greek "their injustice" in 5:6 probably reflects a one-letter difference in Hebrew.
views.J: Jewish readers connect the scroll to the Torah's curses (Deuteronomy 29) and its measurements to the Holy Place. The woman Wickedness is read as the people's wickedness sent away to Babylon (a general pattern in Jewish reading; no one commentator is cited here). The judgment on thieves and false swearers matches Leviticus 19:11-12 and the Ten Commandments.
views.X: Christians have read the scroll as the law that condemns and the ephah as sin carried away. The woman Wickedness and her house in Shinar are compared with the woman and city called Babylon in Revelation 17-18, by image only. These are receptions.
views.F: Some connect the removal of Wickedness to Babylon in Revelation 17-18 and to the end-time removal of evil from the earth (Zechariah 13:1-2 speaks of removing idols and unclean spirits). Others hold that the vision belongs to the second Temple period only.

deep.h: Why a woman in a basket?
deep.b: Readers have long struggled with the ephah scene. The Hebrew says rish'ah ("wickedness") is a woman, which is a matter of grammar, since nearly all Hebrew abstract nouns are feminine. The vision seems to say that the land's corruption is bottled up and exported. The ephah is a measure of trade, and the lead is used to seal it; the stork is an unclean bird; the destination is Shinar, the land of the first city-building defiance of God (Genesis 11). Four readings are common. First, the woman is a goddess or idol who belonged to Babylon and is sent back. Second, the woman is the sin of the community, which is removed. Third, the woman is the commerce of the land, with its false weights. Fourth, the whole scene is a counterpart to the Temple: the LORD builds his house in Jerusalem, and Wickedness gets a "house" in Shinar. The text gives no key, and each reading explains some details and strains others. Feminist readers have noticed and questioned that evil is a woman here, and others reply that Wisdom and Folly in Proverbs are both women. The Plain English Translation keeps the text and lets the views stand.
deep.refs: Genesis 11:2; Leviticus 11:19; Leviticus 16:21-22; Proverbs 9:1-18; Amos 8:5; Micah 6:10-11; Zechariah 3:9; Zechariah 6:15; Revelation 17:1-6

echoes: Deuteronomy 29:20-21; Exodus 20:7; Leviticus 14:45; Leviticus 19:11-12; Amos 8:5; Micah 6:10-12; Habakkuk 2:9-11; Genesis 10:10; Genesis 11:2; Revelation 17:1-6; Revelation 18:2

settings.what: The vision of the flying scroll
settings.by: Zechariah (the vision); the angel who spoke with him; the LORD in 5:4
settings.to: The people of Judah and Jerusalem, especially those who were stealing or swearing falsely
settings.why: To tell a community that had just been cleansed in the vision of Joshua (3:1-5) that it was bound by the covenant's curses, and that the Temple could not be a refuge for thieves and false oaths. The scroll is the size of the Holy Place, which may suggest that the Temple's standard is going out over the land (the match could be an accident).
views: The curse is aimed at individuals who break the commandments.
The scroll is the covenant's curse, and the vision is a reminder that the new beginning is under the same covenant.

settings.what: The vision of the woman in the ephah
settings.by: Zechariah (the vision); the angel who spoke with him
settings.to: The community of Judah, who needed to see wickedness removed from the land and taken to Babylon
settings.why: To assure the community that the root of its troubles, wickedness itself, would be removed from the land and housed elsewhere. It is the second half of the cleansing begun in 3:9.
views: The woman is a cult figure carried back to Babylon.
The woman is the sin of the people, sent away like the scapegoat.
The ephah points to false measures.

title: Four Chariots and a Crown
sum: The eighth vision answers the first. Four chariots come out from between two mountains of bronze, with red, black, white and dappled horses. The angel says they are the four winds of the heavens, going out after presenting themselves before the Lord of the whole earth. The black team goes north, the white team after it, the dappled team south. The "strong" horses are sent to walk the earth. Those that went north "have quieted my spirit in the land of the north" (6:1-8).

Then the word of the LORD comes to Zechariah with a sign act: take silver and gold from three men newly come from Babylon, make crowns and set them on the head of Joshua the high priest. Tell him: "Look, there is a man whose name is Branch," who will branch out, build the temple, bear majesty and sit and rule on his throne. A priest will be on his throne, with a plan of peace between the two. The crowns will be a memorial in the temple, and people from far away will come and build (6:9-15).
readings: Read as the end of the night visions

The first vision found the earth quiet and the second ends with the LORD's spirit at rest in the north. The sequence goes from a question ("how long?") to an answer (the LORD's anger has been spent on Babylon).
Read as a sign for Joshua
Joshua is crowned as a sign, but the Branch of the oracle is another man, in the future, who will be priest and king.
Read as a text about Zerubbabel
The oracle was first about Zerubbabel, who is the temple builder, and was changed or reinterpreted when he disappeared from the record.

views.H: The delegation from Babylon with silver and gold, and the crowning of Joshua, fit the building year of 519. Zerubbabel the Davidic governor and Joshua the high priest are the two leaders, and the book does not say what became of Zerubbabel. The Temple was finished in Darius's sixth year (Ezra 6:15); the Branch's promised throne did not arrive in Zechariah's lifetime.
views.C: The crowning is the most debated passage in 1-8. Some critical scholars think the original had Zerubbabel crowned and a later editor changed it to Joshua. The plural "crowns" (6:11, 14), the singular verb, and "the two of them" (6:13) are the clues. The Greek has "the priest at his right" in 6:13 and renders the names of 6:10 and 6:14 as common words.
views.J: The Targum reads the Branch as the Messiah, who will be revealed and build the temple. Maimonides says the King Messiah will build the Temple (Laws of Kings 11:1), a view that rests on passages like this. Zerubbabel and Joshua are the king and priest of the return.
views.X: Christians read the crowned Joshua (Jesus in Greek) and the Branch as Christ, the priest-king of Hebrews 5-7 and Psalm 110. The Greek "Anatolē" (Dawn) leads to Luke 1:78. Revelation 6:1-8 and 7:1 use related images of horses and the four winds, and Calvin took the Branch as Christ, the one the Father chose to build the temple. The builders from far away are read as the Gentiles (Ephesians 2:13). These are receptions.
views.F: Dispensationalist and many premillennial readings take the Branch as Christ at his return, building a future temple and ruling as priest-king (compare Ezekiel 40-48). Others hold that the temple of 6:12-15 is the church. A third reading takes the passage to be fulfilled in the second Temple and Zerubbabel.

deep.b: The law did not allow a priest to be king, or a king to be priest (the king's attempt in 2 Chronicles 26:16-21 ended in disease). Before the exile, kings and priests were separate. Zechariah has a priest crowned with royal crowns, and an oracle about a Branch who is both on a throne and a priest on his throne. Three explanations run through the scholarship. First, the crowning of Joshua is a sign act pointing to a coming king, and the "man" of 6:12 is a different person (so the text as it stands). Second, the oracle was first about Zerubbabel, the Davidic governor, and it was applied to Joshua when Zerubbabel disappeared. Third, the book looks forward to a rule where priest and king are separate but joined in peace ("between the two of them"). After the exile the high priest became the main leader of the community, and in 140 or 141 BC the Hasmonean Simon was confirmed as leader and high priest (1 Maccabees 14:41-47), which is often seen as the later form of the same pattern. Christians saw in the verse the priest-king after the order of Melchizedek (Psalm 110:4; Hebrews 7).
deep.refs: Psalm 110:1-4; 2 Chronicles 26:16-21; Zechariah 3:8; Zechariah 4:14; 1 Maccabees 14:41-47; Hebrews 5:5-10; Hebrews 7

echoes: Jeremiah 23:5; Jeremiah 33:15; Isaiah 4:2; Haggai 2:23; Psalm 110:1-4; Revelation 6:1-8; Revelation 7:1; Job 1:6; Ezra 1:6; Hebrews 5:5-10; Luke 1:78; Ephesians 2:13

settings.what: The vision of the four chariots
settings.by: Zechariah (the vision); the angel who spoke with him
settings.when: The night of 15 February 519 BC; the eighth and last of the visions
settings.why: To close the series by telling the people that the LORD has sent his forces to all the earth and that the one that matters for them, the north, has been dealt with. It answers the first vision's quiet world with a world in motion under God.
views: The anger against Babylon is satisfied.
A sign of the LORD's rule
The four teams show the LORD's control of the earth in every direction.

settings.what: The crowning of Joshua and the word about the Branch
settings.by: The LORD of Armies, through Zechariah
settings.to: Zechariah (to act), Joshua (to be crowned), the delegates Heldai, Tobiah and Jedaiah and Josiah son of Zephaniah, and the people of Judah
settings.when: Undated; placed after the night visions in the same year, 519 BC, when the delegation had arrived from Babylon with gifts
settings.why: To tell the delegation and the community that their gift would become a memorial in the Temple, and that the high priest crowned that day was a sign of a coming Branch who would build the Temple and rule. The final line, "if you really listen," makes the promise conditional on obedience.
views: The act marks Joshua's rank as the leader of the community.
The original oracle concerned the governor.
A word about a coming king
The Branch is the future Messiah.

traditions.q: Is the Branch who will "also be a priest on that throne" (Zechariah 6:13) Christ, and what does it show about his offices?
views: The Catechism (436) speaks of Christ as prophet, priest and king. Hebrews 7-8 reads his priesthood as a priest-king like Melchizedek.
The Heidelberg Catechism (Q&A 31) says Christ is anointed as prophet, priest and king. Calvin reads 6:12-13 of Christ, whom the Father chose to build the temple.

Arno Gaebelein says the Branch who is a priest on the throne is the Lord Jesus Christ. He says Christ now builds a spiritual temple of living stones, and that when he comes again another temple will be built. The Dallas Theological Seminary statement (Article VI) calls Jesus Israel's Messiah-King.

title: Was It for Me?
sum: Almost two years later, on 7 December 518 BC, a delegation from Bethel (or sent to Bethel; the Hebrew is hard) comes with a question for the priests and prophets of the Temple: should we go on weeping in the fifth month, as we have done for so many years? (7:1-3).

The LORD's word comes to Zechariah as a question back: "For these seventy years you fasted and mourned in the fifth month and the seventh. Did you really fast for me, for me?" And when you eat and drink, is it not for yourselves? The earlier prophets had a different message: judge with true justice, show loyal love and compassion, do not oppress the widow, the fatherless, the foreigner or the poor, do not plan harm. The ancestors gave a defiant shoulder, made their hearts flint, and the LORD scattered them (7:4-14).

views.H: The date, 7 December 518, falls about three years before the Temple was finished and 22 months after the visions. The fasts mark the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 (2 Kings 25; Jeremiah 41). The question shows a community near the end of the Temple building wondering whether its mourning should end.
views.C: Scholars notice that 7:1-8:23 forms a unit with its own dating and its own frame (7:2-3 and 8:18-23). Some see the earlier-prophets speech as shaped by the editors of the book, close to the language of Jeremiah and Nehemiah 9. Others find it original. The Greek of 7:2-3 differs strongly.
views.J: Jewish tradition (a general description; the Talmud passage below is the source) kept the fast days in the calendar and read Zechariah 7-8 as the reason for the fast of Av and the fasts of the four months. The Talmud (Rosh Hashanah 18b) takes 8:19 to mean that the fasts are feasts in times of peace.
views.X: Christians read 7:5-6 with Isaiah 58 and Matthew 6:16-18: fasting must be for God and joined to justice and mercy. Chrysostom taught that fasting must go with giving to the poor: in his Homilies on Matthew (77, section 6, in the New Advent numbering) he says that fasting without almsgiving is not so much as counted for fasting. The list of the widow, the fatherless, the foreigner and the poor became a standing Christian demand (James 1:27). These are receptions.
views.F: The chapter makes no promise about the end. The "still to come" lens is not used for chapter 7.

deep.h: A fast the LORD did not ask for
deep.b: The Law requires only one fast, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29-31; Leviticus 23:27). The four fasts mentioned here are a creation of the exile, to remember the siege, the breach, the burning of the Temple and the murder of Gedaliah. Zechariah's question is the question every ritual of mourning faces when the cause is removed. The prophet does not say the fasts were wrong. He asks to whom they were directed. The answer given in 7:9-10, and repeated in 8:16-17, is that what the LORD asked all along, through the earlier prophets, was justice and loyal love, and no fast replaces those.

echoes: Isaiah 58:3-7; Joel 2:12-13; Matthew 6:16-18; Luke 18:12; Proverbs 1:24-28; Jeremiah 7:6; Jeremiah 22:3; Nehemiah 9:29-30; Deuteronomy 10:18; Amos 5:21-24; Micah 6:8; 2 Kings 25:8-9; Jeremiah 41:1-3

settings.what: The question about fasting, and the first reply
settings.by: A delegation from Bethel (Sharezer, Regem-melech and their men) asks; the LORD of Armies answers through Zechariah
settings.to: The delegation asks the priests of the house of the LORD of Armies and the prophets; the reply is to "all the people of the land and the priests"
settings.when: 7 December 518 BC (the fourth day of the ninth month, Kislev, the fourth year of Darius), while the Temple was nearing completion
settings.why: The community asked whether to stop the mourning for the Temple's destruction now that a new Temple was rising. The LORD answers with a question that turns the fast, and the feast, from a ritual into a test of motive. It sets up the long answer of 8:1-23 and gives the book a second theme beside the Temple: how the community lives.
views: Bethel sent two men with a question for the Temple's priests.
The Hebrew may mean "the house of God sent," which would make the question from within Jerusalem.

settings.what: What the earlier prophets said, and what happened
settings.by: The LORD of Armies, through Zechariah
settings.to: The people of the land and the priests, the same hearers as 7:5
settings.why: To remind a community that has been asking about ritual that the earlier prophets' call was to justice, loyal love and care for the powerless, that the ancestors refused it, and that the exile was the result. The hearers are told what the ancestors had refused so that they will not repeat it.
views: A reminder of the earlier prophets
The speech recalls Jeremiah, Isaiah and others.
Some critics see the speech as shaped to match Deuteronomistic and Jeremianic language.

traditions.q: Should Christians fast, and what is fasting for (Zechariah 7:5-6)?
views: Fasting, prayer and almsgiving are the three chief forms of penance, and Lent and each Friday are set apart as times of heightened penitential practice (Catechism 1434, 1438). The motive is conversion of heart, as the prophets ask, and not only outward discipline.

Fasting is a good discipline but earns nothing: the Augsburg Confession (Article 26) says it does not condemn fasting in itself but the rules that prescribe certain days and foods, and it says the body is disciplined not to merit grace or make satisfaction for sins.

Calvin teaches fasting with prayer in times of public crisis and as private discipline, and warns against superstitious rules (Institutes 4.12.14-21). The Westminster Confession (21.5) lists "solemn fastings" among the parts of religious worship.

Orthodox Christians fast on Wednesdays, in memory of the betrayal of Christ, and on Fridays, in memory of his crucifixion and death. The Orthodox Church in America says that the purpose of fasting is not to "give up" things or to do something "sacrificial."

title: Fasts Become Feasts
sum: The answer comes in a run of oracles, each opening "The LORD of Armies says this." The LORD is jealous for Zion with a great jealousy and has returned to live in Jerusalem, which will be called the City of Truth. Old men and women will sit again in the squares, with children playing around them. If it seems too wonderful to the remnant, will it seem too wonderful to the LORD? He will save his people from east and west, and they will be his people and he their God, in truth and in righteousness (8:1-8).

The builders are told to be strong. The bad years, when there were no wages and neighbor was set against neighbor, will give way to a sowing in peace. The house of Judah and the house of Israel were a curse; they will be a blessing. What the LORD planned for harm he now plans for good, and he commands: speak the truth, judge with true justice, plan no harm, love no false oath (8:9-17). The four fasts will become feasts, and the nations will come in streams to ask the LORD's favor in Jerusalem, until ten men from every language take hold of one Jew's robe and say, "We want to go with you, for we have heard that God is with you" (8:18-23).

views.H: The ten oracles come in the fourth year of Darius (518 BC), probably as the answer given on or soon after 7 December. The Temple would be finished in Darius's sixth year. The bad years (8:10) are those of Haggai 1. The nations' coming (8:20-23) had no counterpart in the Persian period, though Jews did live in many lands.
views.C: Scholars treat 8:1-23 as a collection of sayings. Some view 8:9-13 as a part of the Temple-building appeal, and 8:14-17 as a rule for the community. The chapter's frame is the fasting question (7:1-3; 8:18-19). The Greek has "five cities into one" at 8:21. The Dead Sea scroll 4Q80 preserves a few phrases of 8:2-7.
views.J: The promise that fasts will become feasts is the basis of the discussion in Rosh Hashanah 18b: in times of peace the four fasts are festive. The four fasts are still kept (17 Tammuz, 9 Av, 3 Tishri and 10 Tevet). 8:23 has been read as the world's honor for Israel and the Torah; the tassels on the robe's corner (Numbers 15:38) fit.
views.X: Christians have heard in 8:20-23 the Gentiles coming to the God of Israel through the church (Acts 2:5-11; Romans 11), and in 8:16 the apostle's command to speak truth (Ephesians 4:25). The restoration of the old people sitting in the squares is read as the peace of the kingdom. These are receptions.
views.F: 8:20-23 is read as still to come: the Jewish people honored among the nations (Jewish and many Christian premillennial readings), the nations' pilgrimage to Jerusalem in the age to come (14:16), or the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:24-26). Others see in it the church's mission to the world.

deep.h: Ten sayings of "The LORD of Armies says this"
deep.b: Chapter 8 is built from sayings that all begin "The LORD of Armies says this" (8:2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 14, 19, 20, 23), ten in all. Each is a short promise or command. They are arranged as a movement: the LORD's return and jealousy (8:2-3); peace in the squares (8:4-5); the remnant's doubt (8:6); the ingathering (8:7-8); the builders' encouragement (8:9-13); the LORD's unchanged plan, now for good (8:14-17); the fasts as feasts (8:18-19); and the nations (8:20-23). The structure leads from the LORD to Zion, from Zion to the people, and from the people to the world, which is the direction the book has been moving since 1:3.
deep.refs: Zechariah 1:3; Zechariah 1:16; Zechariah 2:10-11; Zechariah 7:5; Zechariah 8:2-23; Isaiah 2:2-4; Micah 4:1-3

echoes: Isaiah 2:2-4; Micah 4:1-3; Isaiah 65:20-25; Lamentations 2:11; Lamentations 5:14; Genesis 12:2-3; Genesis 18:14; Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 37:27; Ephesians 4:25; Numbers 15:38-39; Haggai 1:6; Haggai 1:10

settings.what: The LORD's return to Zion and the promise to the remnant
settings.by: The LORD of Armies, through Zechariah
settings.to: The remnant of the people in Jerusalem and Judah (8:6)
settings.when: The same day or soon after 7 December 518 BC
settings.why: To answer "is this too good to be true?" with the LORD's jealousy and presence. The hearers were few, poor and doubtful, and had been asking whether to keep mourning. The first sayings tell them the mourning is out of date because the LORD has already returned.

settings.what: The call to be strong and the rule of life
settings.by: The LORD of Armies, through Zechariah
settings.to: The builders and the community, "you who hear these words in these days from the mouths of the prophets"
settings.when: 518 BC, with the Temple nearing completion
settings.why: To strengthen the builders by contrasting the bad years with the blessing now promised, and to give them commands that decide whether they will keep it: truth, justice, no planning of harm, no false oath.
views: 8:9-13 speaks to those still at work on the Temple.
8:14-17 sets out what the LORD requires of the community.

settings.what: The fasts become feasts, and the nations come
settings.by: The LORD of Armies, through Zechariah
settings.to: The house of Judah (8:19), and through the promise the nations (8:20-23)
settings.when: 518 BC, as the final reply to the delegation
settings.why: To answer the original question completely: the four fasts will not simply stop, they will turn into joy, and the nation that asked about its mourning will be sought out by others. The reply asks the nation to love truth and peace, and shows the nation to be the one the nations will come to.

traditions.q: Who are the "ten men" and the "Jew" of Zechariah 8:23, and how do the churches relate the church to Israel?
views: The church draws life from the root of Israel (Nostra Aetate 4).
Calvin, on 8:23, reads the nations as drawn to worship God by the preaching of the truth, with the Jews leading because God presided over them.

The Dallas Theological Seminary statement says the church "is distinct from Israel" (Article XIII) and that Christ at his return will "restore Israel to her own land" (Article XX). Gaebelein reads 8:20-23 as a picture of the whole world turning to God, with the Jew no longer dishonored among the Gentiles but a messenger of the King to the nations.

The UMJC Statement of Faith does not comment on this verse. It says Messiah's community is "a single community expressed in diverse forms within the Jewish community and among the nations," and that "Israel and the nations will be united under Messiah's rule forever."
